title: Haryana Destroys Unsafe Paneer as Diwali Sweet Checks Intensify
excerpt: Gurugram officials destroyed 125 kg of unfit paneer and sent eight samples for testing, as FSSAI-ordered festive raids target adulterated khoya, paneer and sweets across the region.
body:
• Food safety officials in Gurugram seized and destroyed about 125 kg of foul-smelling paneer found unfit for consumption on October 26, and collected eight samples of paneer, khoa and sweets for laboratory testing.
  • In neighbouring Mewat, officials have seized and destroyed more than 10,000 kg of adulterated paneer in recent months across about 50 raids at production hubs.
  • The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India directed all states on September 29 to intensify inspections and on-the-spot testing during Navratri and Diwali.
  • For shoppers buying mithai for Diwali on November 8: buy from reliable sellers, check packaging and expiry details, and avoid sweets or dairy with unusual smell, colour or texture.

Food safety officials in Gurugram destroyed about 125 kg of paneer found unfit for consumption during an inspection on October 26, according to Jazzbaat24. The joint operation by the Gurugram food safety department and the chief minister's flying squads covered several locations, including Sadar Bazaar Mandi, Pataudi Chowk and the Bhagwan Parshuram Vatika area, and officials said foul-smelling paneer was discovered at two shops and destroyed on the spot.

The Haryana action is one part of a wider festive enforcement drive. With Diwali falling on November 8, 2026, demand for sweets, milk products and ghee rises sharply, and regulators say that surge creates greater risk of adulteration and the circulation of unsafe or counterfeit goods.

What the Gurugram team took for testing

Apart from destroying the unsafe paneer, the inspection team collected eight food samples for examination: four samples of paneer, one sample of khoa and three samples of sweets, Jazzbaat24 reported. The samples were to be sent to the state food testing laboratory to determine whether they meet prescribed quality and safety standards.

Officials said further action against the establishments would depend on the laboratory findings. If the samples are found to violate the standards, legal proceedings may be initiated under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The results of those tests were awaited, and no conclusion had been announced on the sampled products.

"The samples were to be sent to the state food testing laboratory to determine whether they meet prescribed quality and safety standards."

A supply chain that reaches Delhi

The scale reported nearby is larger. In Mewat, officials have seized and destroyed more than 10,000 kg of adulterated paneer in recent months, with around 50 raids conducted in areas identified as production hubs, according to a Times of India report carried by NewsPoint. Officials said the supply chain extends to Jaipur, Mathura, Gurugram, Faridabad and Delhi.

In Delhi alone, food safety teams destroyed more than 4,100 kg of suspected adulterated khoya and paneer during enforcement action last month, the same report said, while samples of khoya, paneer, chhena and ghee were being collected from markets for testing.

The national order behind the raids

The state actions follow a national directive. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) directed state and Union Territory authorities on September 29 to step up surveillance, inspections and on-the-spot testing during Navratri and Diwali, according to LatestLY's report of the ANI dispatch. The directive, issued in a letter by Dr Amit Sharma, Executive Director (Compliance), was marked "most important" and told officials to prioritise milk and milk products, sweets, snacks and savouries, edible oils, beverages and ghee.

Authorities were also told to deploy Food Safety on Wheels mobile testing vans at prominent marketplaces where available, and to record inspection, sampling and outcome data in real time on FSSAI's FoSCoS and FoSCoRIS systems. The list of commodities can be adjusted for local consumption patterns, including kuttu atta and singhada atta in northern and western regions.

What shoppers should do

For families in India buying sweets to share, and for diaspora readers ordering festive boxes to send home, the practical guidance from officials and consumer advice in the reports is consistent. Purchase dairy products and sweets from reliable sellers, check packaging and expiry details where applicable, and avoid products with unusual smells, colours or textures, Jazzbaat24 reported officials as advising.

Consumer guidance published ahead of Diwali adds specifics for loose and packaged sweets: check the manufacturing or packing date and best-before information, inspect packaging for damage or leaking seals, ask when loose sweets were prepared and how they were stored, and buy perishable milk-based sweets only in quantities that can be consumed within their recommended storage period. If a product appears unsafe, do not taste it to check its quality; keep the packaging and bill and report it to the seller or the state food safety department.

Inspections in Gurugram will continue, officials said, and food business operators were warned against selling products that fail to meet prescribed standards. The outcome of the eight Gurugram samples will determine whether the shops inspected in October face further action.
